title: Small, role-shaped interfaces
idea: The Interface Segregation Principle (ISP) says no client should depend on methods it does not use, so you split wide interfaces into small role interfaces.
points: Shape each interface around one client's need, not around one implementing class.
Symptom: implementations full of empty methods or `UnsupportedOperationException` stubs.
A class may implement several role interfaces; each client sees only its slice.
ISP turns runtime crashes into compile errors: the wrong object cannot be passed.

hero.title: Clients see only the role they use

steps.caption: Start from the clients. `ReportViewer` only reads; `RetentionJob` only deletes.
Each client gets an interface cut to its need: `DocumentReader` for one, `DocumentWriter` for the other.
`BucketStore` can do both, so it implements both roles. One class, two narrow views.
`LegalArchive` is read-only, so it implements only `DocumentReader`. No stub methods, no surprise throws.
Handing the archive to `RetentionJob` no longer compiles. The type system blocks the bug before it ships.

code.title: The problem
code.caption: One wide `DocumentStore` forces a read-only archive to fake its writes. The purge job compiles, then crashes.

walk.text: `DocumentStore` bundles reading and writing into one contract that every store must sign.
`BucketStore` supports every method, so the wide interface fits it well.
`LegalArchive` cannot write, so it throws from methods it was forced to declare.
`RetentionJob` only needs `delete`, yet its parameter type accepts any store.
The compiler accepts both stores. The archive fails only at runtime, in production.

code.title: The fix
code.caption: Split by role: readers and writers. Each class implements only what it can honour.

walk.text: Reading and changing become two roles. `RetentionJob` still sees `write`; split only if a client needs delete alone.
`BucketStore` implements both roles and validates input. `read` returns `Optional` instead of null.
`LegalArchive` implements only reading. It has nothing left to fake.
Each client asks for the narrowest role in its constructor, then rejects null.
The viewer works with both stores. Passing the archive to the purge job fails to compile.

pitfalls: Stubbing methods with `UnsupportedOperationException` hides an ISP violation until a caller hits it at runtime.
Splitting into one-method interfaces nobody asks for creates clutter; split only by real clients.
Adding an abstract method to a widely used interface breaks every implementer; add a new role.

quiz.q: A new `AuditTool` must list all keys, but `LegalArchive` cannot list. Best design?
options: A new `KeyLister` interface, implemented only by stores that list
Give `listKeys()` a default method in `DocumentReader` returning null
quiz.why: A new role interface serves the new client without touching existing implementers. Throwing or returning null recreates the trap; casting couples the tool to one class.

takeaway: Interfaces belong to their clients: give each client only what it calls.
